This page explains what the Open Performance Data Initiative (OPDI) publishes,
how the data are organised in files, and which release to use. The pages
below it explain how to read the data, what every column means, what changed
between releases and where the data have limits.

```{r status}
#| results: asis
#| echo: false
if (v2_current) {
  cat(
    "::: {.callout-note appearance=\"simple\"}\n",
    "**Current release: ", cfg$release, ".** It covers the days ",
    rel$coverage_text(cfg), ". The previous release, ", cfg$previous_release,
    ", stays available: see [Previous release ", cfg$previous_release, "](v0.0.2.qmd).\n",
    ":::\n", sep = "")
} else {
  cat(
    "::: {.callout-note appearance=\"simple\"}\n",
    "**Release ", cfg$release, " is the upcoming release.** This section describes it. ",
    "Its files are being produced, starting with the days from ",
    rel$day_text(cfg$release_coverage$start), " onwards. Until they are available, use ",
    "release ", cfg$current_release, ", which covers ",
    portal_labels$month_range(cfg$coverage$start, cfg$coverage$end),
    ": see [Previous release ", cfg$previous_release, "](v0.0.2.qmd).\n",
    ":::\n", sep = "")
}
```

## What is published

OPDI starts from the position reports that aircraft broadcast by radio. The
reports are received by the [OpenSky Network](https://opensky-network.org/), a
network of ground receivers run by volunteers, universities and other
organisations. OPDI groups the reports of one aircraft into flights and
describes each flight in two ways.

- The **flight list** has one row per flight. A row gives the aircraft, its
  call sign, the departure and destination airports, the first and last time
  the flight was seen, and the main times of the flight, such as the take-off
  and landing times and the runways used.
- The **flight events** have one row per event. An **event** is a moment in a
  flight with a time and a position, for example the take-off, the top of
  climb, the crossing of a flight level or the entry into a holding pattern.
  Each row also carries the **measurements** taken at that event, for example
  the distance flown since the start of the flight, and the columns of its
  flight, so that one row can be used on its own.

A list of every column is on the [Data dictionary](dictionary.qmd) page. How
each column and event is computed is explained in [Methods](../methods/index.qmd).

## The daily files

Release `r cfg$release` has two files for each day:

| File | One row per | Size of one day |
|---|---|---|
| `flight_list/flight_list_YYYYMMDD.parquet` | flight | about 7 MB |
| `flight_events/flight_events_YYYYMMDD.parquet` | event | about 410 MB |

`YYYYMMDD` is the date, for example `20260614` for 14 June 2026. The sizes
were measured on that day, which has 175,615 flights and 6,773,617 events
worldwide.

The files are in **Parquet**, a file format that stores data by column and
that most data tools read: Python (pandas, pyarrow, polars), R (arrow),
DuckDB, Spark and Trino. A program that reads only some columns, or only some
rows, reads only part of the file.

Two small files help to find data:

- a **flight index** per month, `index/flight_index_YYYYMM.parquet`, with one
  row per flight of the month and the name of the daily file that holds it;
- a **catalogue**, `catalogue.parquet`, with one row per published day: the
  number of flights and events, the time of the first and last event, the
  file sizes and the versions of the methods used.

Their columns are listed on the [Data dictionary](dictionary.qmd#flight-index-and-catalogue)
page.

## Which day a flight belongs to

A flight belongs to the day on which it was **first seen**, in UTC. That date
is the column `dof` (date of flight). The two files of a day hold the flights
first seen that day and **all** their events, also the events after midnight.
A flight that takes off at 23:30 UTC and lands at 02:00 UTC the next day is
therefore in the files of the day it took off, with its landing.

A small number of events belong to a track that has no row in the flight list
(3,442 of 6,773,617 events, or 0.05%, on 14 June 2026). They are published in
the file of the day their track started, with empty flight columns.

## Coverage

Release `r cfg$release` covers the whole world: every flight that the OpenSky
Network received. Release `r cfg$previous_release` covered a box around Europe
only. Reception is not the same everywhere: it depends on where receivers
are, and it is thin over the oceans and near the ground at many airports. [Limitations](limitations.qmd#ads-b-reception)
explains what this means for the data.

## How to get the data

- **Through Trino.** Trino is a database engine that runs SQL queries
  directly on files. The OPDI files are available as tables on the OpenSky
  Network's Trino instance. This is the quickest way to select a few flights
  or to count over many days without downloading anything.
- **As files.** The daily files can be downloaded and read with Python, R,
  DuckDB or any other tool that reads Parquet.

[Access](access.qmd) gives the names of the tables, the addresses of the files
and example queries for both.
